analysis.one_liner: Gives antitrust enforcers and unions more information and time to challenge mergers that hurt workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2024 and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsors before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the government reviews large corporate mergers. Companies seeking a merger would have to disclose how many employees are covered by union contracts, internal studies about the deal's effects on jobs and labor markets, and any recent labor law penalties. The antitrust agencies would have to keep watching mergers after they close to see if they raised prices, cut wages, or shipped jobs overseas, and unions would get formal notice and the right to submit evidence, which could extend the review period by 60 days. It also orders two government studies on consolidation's effects on manufacturing and worker bargaining power.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies involved in large mergers — especially union members — would gain advance notice and a formal channel to tell antitrust enforcers about planned layoffs, offshoring, or union-busting before a deal closes. Consumers could also benefit if agency scrutiny of post-merger price increases deters harmful deals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Union workers and employees of merging firms

how_it_helps.text: Companies filing for merger review must disclose the number and percentage of employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement, contact information for affected unions, and internal studies analyzing the deal's effects on labor markets or employees.

Filings must include the five largest overlapping job categories, employee counts, the local areas workers commute from, and any wage-and-hour, NLRB, or OSHA penalties against either company in the prior five years.

The FTC and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division must regularly monitor consummated mergers under investigation to determine whether they lessened competition, created monopoly power, or reduced worker bargaining power — with evidence including higher prices, lower quality, wage cuts, plant closings, elimination of union-covered jobs, offshoring, or unfair labor practices.

Unions get official notice of mergers affecting their members and the right to submit documents and information to the agencies, which must respond in writing; a union submission can extend the 30-day merger waiting period by 60 days.

The Comptroller General would conduct studies on consolidation in manufacturing since 1975 — including effects on unionized workforces, prices, and offshoring — and on rising concentration in labor markets, with $5 million authorized.

analysis.who_pays: Companies pursuing large mergers would bear the cost of more extensive filings, longer waiting periods when unions raise concerns, and a higher chance of post-close investigations and enforcement, including possible unwind of deals that harm workers or competition.

drawbacks.text: Longer waiting periods and heavier disclosure requirements add time, legal, and compliance costs to merger transactions, and business groups generally argue this slows deals that are often benign or beneficial to efficiency.

The bill directs agencies to treat offshoring and labor practices as antitrust evidence, which critics of such approaches argue stretches competition law beyond its traditional purpose of protecting consumers and markets.
The monitoring mandate requires ongoing agency surveillance of closed mergers without new appropriations specified beyond the $5 million for the studies, raising questions about enforcement capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and communities affected by mergers, the bill's main value is information and a voice: unions would learn about deals before they close and could trigger a longer review with evidence of planned job cuts. The costs fall on merging companies as filing burden and deal delay, and there is a real design question about whether antitrust law is the right tool for policing offshoring and labor practices. The bill does not block any merger outright; it changes what enforcers know and how long they can look.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2024, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The action history shows no further action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations considering large mergers are better off, since merger reviews remain unchanged: they keep the shorter waiting periods, the limited disclosure, and no formal role for unions or post-close monitoring.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee or floor action, the bill never drew enough attention for a partisan lineup to form.

industries.industry: Large corporations pursuing mergers and acquisitions
industries.note: The bill would require detailed labor-market disclosures, allow unions to extend the review window by 60 days, and subject closed mergers to ongoing antitrust monitoring, raising deal costs and enforcement risk. Their gain under the status quo is faster, quieter approvals.

Unions would get mandatory notice when their members' employers merge, a formal right to submit evidence, and a 60-day extension of the review period — giving organized labor its first explicit seat in the merger-review process.

A required retrospective study would examine consolidation's effects on unionized workforces, prices, and offshoring in manufacturing, which could feed future enforcement; the study itself imposes no obligations.
